{"id": "6:122/q07", "question": "Is the life in the verse figurative or a real higher life?", "turns_on": "Whether familiar life and death are solely a comparison or indicate a distinct level of actual life.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q07/p1", "position": "Death and revival are figurative names for error and guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī places the metaphor in the predicate 'life,' while attribution of the gift to God remains literal; he distinguishes metaphors in both predicate and attribution and describes disparagement by treating existence as nonexistence. Al-Suyūṭī calls revival a concordant metaphor. Abū Ḥayyān, Asad, and Study Quran state the spiritual metaphor; Ibn ʿĀshūr develops two complete figurative scenes."}, {"id": "6:122/q07/p2", "position": "The believer's spiritual life and light are actual higher realities.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues from the good life promised in 16:97, the deficient hearts, eyes and ears of unbelievers in 7:179, and the spirit supporting believers in 58:22. He says faith yields higher perception and will, an enduring life protected by God and immersed in divine love. Ibn ʿArabī, as quoted by Bursawī, progressively denies created things independent acts, life, and existence; Bursawī says only God is unqualifiedly alive."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q08", "question": "What inward states do death, revival and light describe?", "turns_on": "The inward sources locate death in separation, ignorance, self-regard or desire, and distinguish several effects and signs of revived life.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q08/p1", "position": "Ignorance, separation or veiling is death; knowing, loving and drawing near to God is life and light.", "reasons": "Sahl calls ignorance death and knowledge life; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ makes separation death and connection light. Al-Qāshānī describes the soul veiled by its attributes and revived through knowledge and love of the Real or divine disclosure; graded light comes as guidance, divine attributes or sustaining presence. Bursawī's people of spiritual reality add self-following versus divine love, and gnosis that outlasts bodily life, supported by a Prophetic report and Ḥāfiẓ's verse. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes enduring love and higher perception; his treatment of Joseph says love purifies motives beyond fear and hope, and divine love guides beautiful acts."}, {"id": "6:122/q08/p2", "position": "Death is the self or reliance on one's own acts; life is the awakened, needy heart.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ contrasts a living self and dead heart with extinguishing the self and enlivening the heart by lights of nearness. Jaʿfar says reliance on obedience dies through supplication and apology; an unnamed authority contrasts seeing one's deeds with seeing one's need. Al-Qāsim compares awakening's light to bodily spirits; al-Qannāʾ calls it gnosis rather than biological life and describes annihilation from invocations and life in God."}, {"id": "6:122/q08/p3", "position": "Revival makes a person a guide to others and grants abiding life through God's light.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar says the one revived by God becomes a guide to strangers and the lost while the desire-following person lacks divine nearness. Al-Jurayrī says the servant enlivened by divine lights never truly dies; abandonment is never true life. Bursawī says one alive with love does not die and preserves the believer-alive-in-both-abodes report."}, {"id": "6:122/q08/p4", "position": "Spiritual life shows itself in remembrance, watchfulness, detachment and preparation for death.", "reasons": "Shāh al-Kirmānī gives intimacy after loneliness, fullness of the Real through constant remembrance, and awe from pure watchfulness. Shāh names transience of the world, preparation for death, and tears at the afterlife as signs of a heart's light. Bursawī's report from the King of Kerman gives seclusion from people, calling to God and remembrance by tongue and heart; these formulations differ in their signs."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q09", "question": "What does the fāʾ in «فَأَحْيَيْنَٰهُ» do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q09/p1", "position": "It is conjunctive.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reads the fāʾ as joining the revival to the prior state."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q10", "question": "What theological point is drawn from God giving life and light?", "turns_on": "How the divine act of giving guidance is described: creation of faith and motives, distinct modes of guidance, or the reported primordial distribution of light.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q10/p1", "position": "God creates faith, guidance and the motives behind belief or unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says life and light are knowledge and guidance explicitly given by God; a person seeking knowledge but receiving ignorance has the contrary produced in him. Explaining each mistaken judgment by an earlier mistaken judgment regresses unless some ignorance is created externally. His school's account of God-created motives also governs the adorned deeds."}, {"id": "6:122/q10/p2", "position": "God's guidance includes created direction and revealed direction, with different outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes created direction of each being toward its form, appointed acts and lifespan (20:50; 87:2–3) from legislative guidance to true belief and righteous action with promised reward and punishment; the latter can merely show the road (76:3) or bring one to it (7:176)."}, {"id": "6:122/q10/p3", "position": "A report says God created beings in darkness, then sprinkled His light upon them.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites Aḥmad's Musnad: whoever received the light was guided, while whoever missed it went astray."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q11", "question": "What distinctive word choices and omissions sharpen the two scenes?", "turns_on": "Which asymmetries of attribution, number and ellipsis explain the comparison's force.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q11/p1", "position": "The illuminated believer is credited to God and benefits others; the dark counterpart is settled in varied darknesses.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān observes explicit divine attribution of the believer's benefits, no equivalent agent attribution for the dark figure, plural darknesses for varied unbelief, and public illumination benefiting others. Biqāʿī says if even the ideal likeness is rooted in darkness, the represented person is worse; al-Ṭabrisī says physical light and knowledge alike guide on a road. Bursawī explicitly says God gives a great light alongside the life."}, {"id": "6:122/q11/p2", "position": "The verse omits matching details on each side, inviting completion of the paired images.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says darkness is mentioned with the second image but implied in the first, while adornment is said second and implied first. Ibn ʿĀshūr says light and walking imply death in darkness for the other side; the final clause supplies the reason for the persistent error."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q12", "question": "What is the light given to the revived person?", "turns_on": "Whether the gift denotes faith itself, scripture, the understanding produced by faith, eschatological light, an Imam, or revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q12/p1", "position": "It is faith, Islam, religion, or divine guidance.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it faith guiding among people. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Kalbī and Ibn Zayd give guidance, religion, faith or Islam; al-Wāḥidī explicitly treats these as equivalent. Al-Baghawī cites 2:257, al-Dāmghānī 57:28 and 2:257, and Ibn al-Jawzī 2:257, 24:40 and 57:28. Ibn Kathīr accepts Islam alongside the Qurʾān reading. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers faith; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the context requires divine guidance to true belief and action."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p2", "position": "It is knowledge, wisdom, insight, certainty, or proof that distinguishes truth from error.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū ʿAlī describe wisdom and faith illuminating a Muslim through Islam. Al-Māwardī calls it knowledge toward right conduct; al-Rāzī says coordination with revival makes light a further endowment and prefers a model of acquired theory and sacred insight over bare glosses. Al-Bayḍāwī and Bursawī stress proofs and signs; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says knowledge grows from faith and cites the report that acting on known truth yields unknown knowledge. He rejects faith or Qurʾān as the exact light in this context."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p3", "position": "It is the Qurʾān or God's Book, a clear proof for conduct.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says one believes and practices the Qurʾān; Qatāda says the believer acts by God's Book, receives guidance from it and turns to it. Al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Kathīr preserve the competing scripture and faith glosses; Ibn Kathīr accepts both. Iṣlāḥī connects God's Book to 6:114–119 as the criterion against innovations; Study Quran calls the Quran a possible specific sense."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p4", "position": "It is the believer's light in the hereafter.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī invokes 57:12–13, the light running ahead and at believers' right that hypocrites seek. Al-Qurṭubī reports the same. Abū Ḥayyān rejects taking this light and the darkness here as resurrection light and Hell darkness, despite 57:12 and 66:8."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p5", "position": "It is revelation reaching a soul prepared to receive it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares readiness and revelation to a healthy eye and sunlight; Abū Ḥayyān reports the account but deems Rāzī's philosophical elaboration distant from common Arabic. Study Quran names revelation explicitly."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p6", "position": "Its primary sense is visible radiance; by extension it names what clarifies and guides.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī transmits ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allāh's definition of radiance by which sight reaches visible things; derives the word from fire and nāra/anāra/istanāra, and records figurative use for clear speech and manār as landmarks. Manāra follows the mafʿala pattern from istināra. The verse's faith usage belongs to the extend

ed sense."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p7", "position": "It is acquired reasoning and finally present sacred insight, after the soul receives basic knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī distinguishes capacity, axioms, theoretical reasoning and immediately illuminating sacred insight; he prefers this staged account to the simpler Qurʾān, religion or wisdom glosses, though calls them close. Abū Ḥayyān reports the model but objects that it exceeds normal Arabic usage."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p8", "position": "It is an Imam whom the believer follows.", "reasons": "Imam al-Bāqir, reported in al-Kāfī, glosses the dead as knowing nothing and the light as an Imam. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī accepts this as application to a case while reading the context as guidance to belief and righteous action."}, {"id": "6:122/q12/p9", "position": "It is the beauty of faith.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī records this as a third gloss."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q13", "question": "What does walking by the light among people mean?", "turns_on": "Whether walking chiefly describes guided conduct and a path toward Paradise, or the public reach of the believer's religion and example.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q13/p1", "position": "The believer lives, speaks and acts among people under guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī compares 57:28. Abū Sinān says acting by it; Qatāda says the Book directs deeds; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says faith governs action and speech. Al-Māwardī says walking guided toward Paradise, and al-Baghawī along the straight path. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the believer discerns a dark social path and chooses deeds leading to happiness."}, {"id": "6:122/q13/p2", "position": "The believer publicly displays, spreads or conveys the religion, benefiting others.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī interprets walking as spreading mention of religion. Biqāʿī says deeds, character and speech become visible; Abū Ḥayyān says the light illuminates others as well as its bearer. Iṣlāḥī urges presenting God's light openly so others benefit; Bursawī says the person moves safely among people."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q14", "question": "How do the words «يَمْشِى بِهِۦ فِى ٱلنَّاسِ» attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the walking clause is descriptive or an answer to an implied question, and whether 'among people' belongs to walking or the prior death.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q14/p1", "position": "Yamshī qualifies the light, and fī al-nās attaches to the walking; the bāʾ marks the means or cause.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn makes yamshī an adjective of nūran; Ibn ʿAṭiyya ordinarily attaches fī al-nās to yamshī. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the bāʾ causal and says 'people' in the pictured scene are living members of society, corresponding to the convert's fellow Muslims."}, {"id": "6:122/q14/p2", "position": "The walking clause answers an implied question about what one does with the light.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers this beside its adjectival attachment to nūran."}, {"id": "6:122/q14/p3", "position": "Fī al-nās can attach to kāna maytan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows this alternative, placing 'among people' with the former state."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q15", "question": "What does the verse teach believers to do with the given light?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q15/p1", "position": "Act by God's guidance and carry it among people for their benefit.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says God's light is for seeking guidance and public presentation, never concealment; 6:114–119 supply its scriptural setting. Qatāda says the believer acts by God's Book and returns to it; Abū Sinān says walking means acting. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says insight selects happiness-producing acts. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Islam restores discernment and avoidance of corruption."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q16", "question": "How does «كَمَن مَّثَلُهُۥ فِى ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ» work?", "turns_on": "Whether mathal contributes a description, is semantically extra, or invokes a further implicit comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q16/p1", "position": "Mathal means description, condition, or example: his description is that he remains in darkness.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf compares 47:15, where the following clause supplies Paradise's description. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Samīn make mathaluhu subject and fī al-ẓulumāt predicate. Al-Wāḥidī's grammarians call the person an example; Abū ʿAlī says the likeness's darkness means the person's darkness. Biqāʿī reads example exposing the inner state or a description; Bursawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr read remarkable condition or state. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī supplies an omitted pronoun returning to man."}, {"id": "6:122/q16/p2", "position": "Mathal or mithl is extra in sense: the phrase means 'like one in darkness.'", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī compare extra wording in 5:95 and 42:11; al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī agree. Al-Wāḥidī says mithl and mathal coincide here. Al-Jurjānī cautions that an added word is not itself a metaphor, though an unexpected case created by an added particle may be called figurative, and discusses aspect-dependent addition with 57:29 and Abū ʿAlī's lām example."}, {"id": "6:122/q16/p3", "position": "The sense is 'someone whose likeness, if likened, would be a person in darkness.'", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl offers this analysis, which al-Wāḥidī calls weakest. Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī report it; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī would accept it except for its excessive ellipsis."}, {"id": "6:122/q16/p4", "position": "One reported construal takes the phrase as an imperative 'be,' or likens the person to one wandering in unbelief, ignorance and error.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī transmits both formulations as an alternative view."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q17", "question": "How does the imagery connect to the preceding warning and following verses?", "turns_on": "Which part of the surrounding discourse is used to explain the placement and purpose of the parable.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q17/p1", "position": "It follows the warning at 6:121 against obeying polytheist and satanic arguments by contrasting their darkness with believers' light.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya sees believers ordered to avoid outward and inward sin against unbelievers ruled by desires. Al-Rāzī says a dispute over religion leads into the parable. Biqāʿī reads obedience as return to darkness. Al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭībī link 'if you obey them' to this deterrent. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies disputes over carrion and non-God offerings; Kur'an Yolu echoes 6:121. Iṣlāḥī connects the Book at 6:114–119 to darkness of speculation at 6:116 and 6:119, urging believers past satanic clamour."}, {"id": "6:122/q17/p2", "position": "Its last clause prepares 6:123: adorned wrongdoing continues in leaders' plots that keep people from the Messenger.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī relates attractive deeds to God placing criminals at each town's head. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads 6:123 as another explanatory resumption: leaders' plotting diverts others. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says their plotting in the next verse harms themselves. Muqātil's Abū Jahl report reaches 6:124, where he demands revelation for himself."}, {"id": "6:122/q17/p3", "position": "It unfolds earlier themes of the sūra's opening, reception of truth, and divine protection.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī views 6:100 through the end as developing the opening call to take God as protector and Creator (6:14, 6:100); revival continues the Prophet's commanded submission (6:14) and recalls those who hear versus deaf deniers in darkness (6:36, 6:39). He says restating a proven point in a new style fixes and clarifies it, with al-Ghazālī urging attention to what surrounds repetition. Ibn Kathīr notes the sūra's opening at 6:1, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī 6:36."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q18", "question": "Which other verses illuminate the light and darkness contrast?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison is illuminated chiefly by light/darkness parallels or by passages about a distinct life of believers.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q18/p1", "position": "Qurʾānic parallels repeatedly oppose unbelief and guidance as darkness and light, blindness and sight, or crooked and upright walking.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites 2:257, 67:22, 11:24, 35:19–23 and 6:1. Al-Ṭabrisī cites 13:19 and 35:19 for blindness. Study Quran cites 5:15, 7:157, 14:1, 21:48, 39:22, 42:52, 64:8, 57:12, 66:8 for light, and 2:257, 5:16, 14:5, 33:43, 57:9, 65:11 for coming out of darkness; it points to 6:1 and 24:35. Al-Dāmghānī cites 57:28 and 2:257. Study Quran observes this sūra's fair-seeming deeds at 6:43, 6:108, 6:137; Elmālīlı compares 6:108."}, {"id": "6:122/q18/p2", "position": "The believer's distinct good life is illuminated by 16:97 and related passages.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī invokes 16:97 to distinguish real believerly life, and 7:179 and 58:22 for perfected spiritual faculties and God's spirit; he also notes the hearers/dead contrast at 6:36. Bursawī connects 3:185 and 16:97 to gnosis lasting beyond bodily death."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q19", "question": "What are the darknesses, and why can the person not escape?", "turns_on": "Whether darkness is read directly as unbelief, as ignorance, as the literal grave in the pictured comparison, or as spiritual veiling.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q19/p1", "position": "They are unbelief and misguidance; persistence leaves the person bewildered and unable to find guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies unbelief and error; Qatāda likens it to stumbling without an exit. Al-Wāḥidī transmits al-Kalbī's 'never becomes a believer'; Mujāhid says misguidance lasts. Ibn Kathīr adds ignorance and divergent desires; Biqāʿī traces ignorance to desire to disbelief. Al-Rāzī says entrenched traits seem innate. Abū Ḥayyān says plural darknesses reflect varied unbelief; Bursawī and Kur'an Yolu qualify impossibility as persistence in that state. Ibn Zayd says the person cannot foresee what will befall him."}, {"id": "6:122/q19/p2", "position": "They are ignorance, which bewilders a person and leads to ruin.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī explains the comparison to someone lost while walking in

 the dark. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links it to inability to discern beneficial acts and salvation."}, {"id": "6:122/q19/p3", "position": "On the inward reading, they are the self, its attributes and acts, or separation from God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says these veils prevent emergence; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ describes the darkness of severance from God."}, {"id": "6:122/q19/p4", "position": "The picture is literally the darkness of a grave surrounding a dead person.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says grave darkness fits 'in' and 'exit' literally; the represented case remains polytheism and inability to discern truth or pursue salvation."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q20", "question": "What force does the bāʾ in «لَيْسَ بِخَارِجٍ» add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q20/p1", "position": "It reinforces the settled denial that the person can leave darkness.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says it intensifies the image; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes firm bāʾ-negation from a less fully committed bare laysa, citing numerous Qurʾānic examples. Al-Thaʿlab and al-Mubarrad, as transmitted by al-Suyūṭī, call sentence-initial negation genuine and distinguish it from paired negatives."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q21", "question": "What does «كَذَٰلِكَ» point back to?", "turns_on": "Which earlier act or scene supplies the comparison for 'thus' and how its kāf attaches syntactically.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q21/p1", "position": "It compares the unbelievers' adornment with the believers' faith being made attractive.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Bayḍāwī and Bursawī say each group's condition is likened in the attractiveness of its chosen course; al-Ṭabrisī cites 23:53. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects this in context, though al-Ālūsī reports it as an option."}, {"id": "6:122/q21/p2", "position": "It points to bringing believers to life, or to the unbelievers' remaining in darkness.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn analyzes the kāf as adjective of an omitted verbal noun and reports both estimates. Ibn ʿAṭiyya likewise allows attachment to an implied 'as We revived believers' or to the darker comparison. Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq put kāf in the nominative: 'like what was related to you was adorned.' Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a causal parallel: God equipped believers with light and allowed criminals their chosen error and plotting."}, {"id": "6:122/q21/p3", "position": "It points to the striking adornment itself, explaining the disbelievers' persistence in darkness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reads it as the astonishing cunning embellishment implied by the verb, comparing 2:143; the final sentence answers why intelligent polytheists remained despite proof. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the parable supplies a general model, comparing 13:17 and 29:43, and adornment imprisons them. Al-Ālūsī also allows reference to earlier adornment."}, {"id": "6:122/q21/p4", "position": "It recalls devils inspiring their allies in the preceding warning.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly offers this antecedent alongside prior adornment and the adornment of faith."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q22", "question": "Who makes the unbelievers' deeds attractive?", "turns_on": "Whether the passive is supplied with God, Satan, both at different causal levels, or kept deliberately unspecified.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q22/p1", "position": "Satan or human and jinn devils adorn the deeds by suggestion and deception.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says Satan makes idol worship attractive. The Muʿtazila cite al-Ḥasan; al-Ṭabrisī joins Satan and the self, invoking 6:121. Ibn ʿĀshūr says human devils embellish directly and jinn prompt, invoking 6:137. Kur'an Yolu links the failure of judgment to 6:121. Al-Rāzī argues against Satan as sole source."}, {"id": "6:122/q22/p2", "position": "God does so by creating the motive or by His decree.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī's school argues every act rests on a judgment of greater benefit, whose motive God creates. He rejects Satan as sole agent: tracing Satan's unbelief to another satan gives regress; 6:108 and 6:123 attribute such acts to God. Al-Nasafī cites 6:108, Ibn Kathīr speaks of divine decree and wisdom, and Biqāʿī of a formed disposition. Al-Kashshāf and al-Samīn report the attribution, with 27:4 as evidence."}, {"id": "6:122/q22/p3", "position": "Both attributions work: devils whisper; God creates what occurs.", "reasons": "Bursawī distinguishes creation from Satan's whispering. Elmālīlı says God creates the devils' promptings as they happen, while they mislead. Al-Ālūsī states both modes. Al-Ṭabrisī adds that the passive does not even require a distinct agent, citing idioms of self-admiration and devotion."}, {"id": "6:122/q22/p4", "position": "The passive leaves the agent unspecified to emphasize the occurrence of adornment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the focus is the occurrence, not naming its author; al-Samīn says either God or Satan can be supplied, citing 27:4 and 29:38. Al-Sāmarrāʾī observes that God explicitly claims adorning faith and heavens, whereas desires and evil deeds are usually passive and this verse does not say 'We adorned their evil deeds.'"}]}
{"id": "6:122/q23", "question": "What deeds are made attractive, and what is their effect?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is specifically idolatry and sins, or the general self-approval that veils a person.", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q23/p1", "position": "Their unbelief, idol worship and sins look good to them, so they persist in error.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies polytheists, especially Abū Jahl. Ibn ʿAbbās names idol worship; al-Baghawī names disbelief and disobedience. Al-Ālūsī and Bursawī include many repeated forms of sin; Ibn ʿĀshūr says delight in them explains persistence despite intelligence and proofs. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Elmālīlı say attractive deeds imprison them in darkness and cannot bring escape. Iṣlāḥī relates this to 6:125 and 2:7 and offers reassurance to the Prophet."}, {"id": "6:122/q23/p2", "position": "The passive may include self-admiration of one's own deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī uses Arabic self-regarding idioms to show that no separate beautifier is grammatically necessary. Al-Qāshānī says the veiled see their own acts as good and remain screened by them."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q24", "question": "How is «مَا كَانُوا۟ يَعْمَلُونَ» parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q24/p1", "position": "The clause occupies the passive subject's position; mā has three possible analyses.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says mā can be a relative pronoun, a verbal-noun particle, or an indefinite noun qualified by the following clause; relative and indefinite analyses imply an omitted resumptive."}]}
{"id": "6:122/q25", "question": "What ruling is drawn about offerings or acts directed to jinn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:122/q25/p1", "position": "Rituals or sacrifices performed to win jinn protection or imitate their offerings are shirk.", "reasons": "Bursawī names burning incense, sprinkling rosewater or sacrificing where jinn are suspected; he also condemns sacrifices imitating a rooster or guarding family and property when directed to jinn."}]}
{"id": "6:128/q01", "question": "What is the gathering mentioned here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q01/p1", "position": "The gathering of creatures for judgment at the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Muqatil includes disbelieving humans, devils, and jinn; Mawardi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Elmalili, and others locate it at the resurrection assembly. {"id": "6:128/q02", "question": "Who is included in 'He gathers them all'?", "turns_on": "The scope of the pronoun and the force of 'all.'", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q02/p1", "position": "Jinn and humans, including their allies, are gathered.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies human disbelievers, devils and jinn. {"id": "6:128/q03", "question": "How is 'He gathers them' read?", "turns_on": "Third-person yāʾ versus divine first-person plural nūn.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q03/p1", "position": "Yaḥshuruhum, 'He gathers them,' with yāʾ.", "reasons": "Hafs from Asim is named by Ibn Mujahid and others; Tabarsi and Alusi add Rawh from Yaqub. {"id": "6:128/q06", "question": "Whom does 'company of jinn' address?", "turns_on": "Literal jinn devils versus their close human associates.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q06/p1", "position": "The devils or evil jinn who misled humans.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Baydawi and many later authors identify the addressed jinn as devils. {"id": "6:128/q07", "question": "What does maʿshar mean here?", "turns_on": "Ordinary group or a complete multitude derived from ten.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q07/p1", "position": "A group or class held together by a common bond.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi and Alusi give this sense and plural maʿāshir; Abu Hayyan and Samin cite the prophetic phrase about the prophets and poems by al-Afwah or al-Awdi. {"id": "6:128/q08", "question": "What implicit speech introduces the address, and who speaks?", "turns_on": "Direct divine speech versus passive 'it is said.'", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q08/p1", "position": "God says the address after gathering them.", "reasons": "Razi supplies 'then God says' and treats it as rebuke; Ibn Atiyya and Alusi supply a saying verb. {"id": "6:128/q09", "question": "Why is the jinn assembly addressed publicly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q09/p1", "position": "The call reproaches and exposes the misleaders before all creatures.", "reasons": "Razi says they must admit guilt after defiance; Qurtubi calls it a public reproach of leaders and followers; Abu Hayyan says it brings notoriety; Biqai stresses humiliation when the devils cannot defend themselves. {"id": "6:128/q10", "question": "What does 'you have taken many from humans' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it emphasizes misguidance, followers, or the resulting number of Hell's people.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q10/p1", "position": "The jinn misled many humans and made them their followers.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Farra, Qatada, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Zajjaj, Wahidi and others give this core gloss. {"id": "6:128/q11", "question": "How is 'taken many from humans' construed?", "turns_on": "Misleading action implied versus abundance of followers or enjoyment.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q11/p1", "position": "It can mean amassing human followers, as a commander amasses troops.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, and Alusi use the troop or partisan analogy."}, {"id": "6:128/q11/p2", "position": "Istakthara min means doing much of an action, with misguidance understood.", "reasons": "Tabatabai gives the lexical construction and rejects a physical gathering. {"id": "6:128/q12", "question": "Who are the jinn's human allies?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q12/p1", "position": "Humans who obeyed, followed, or were misled by the jinn.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn al-Jawzi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai and others identify the allies as obedient or misled people. {"id": "6:128/q13", "question": "How does 'from humans' attach to 'their allies'?", "turns_on": "Circumstantial qualifier versus identification of kind.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q13/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial qualifier: their allies were human.", "reasons": "Samin reports this; Bursevi holds that min al-ins modifies awliyāʾuhum as ḥāl."}, {"id": "6:128/q13/p2", "position": "It specifies the human kind among allies who include jinn as well.", "reasons": "Samin offers specification of kind; Alusi allows identification of kind or an omitted descriptive phrase."}]}

{"id": "6:128/q18", "question": "How is the speech and judgment narrated as past?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q18/p1", "position": "The past tense presents the future judgment as certain.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls this eloquent Qur'anic usage; Biqai says God's promise cannot fail; Kuranyolu describes the gathering as if already past."}, {"id": "6:128/q18/p2", "position": "The human response presumes an omitted response from the jinn.", "reasons": "Biqai reconstructs it from the following sūra's dialogue at 7:38."}]}

{"id": "6:128/q20", "question": "What appointed term had they reached?", "turns_on": "Death, resurrection, the limit of enjoyment or respite, or an acquired spiritual state.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q20/p1", "position": "Death, sometimes with the grave, is the appointed term.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and a majority in Abu Hayyan give this gloss. {"id": "6:128/q21", "question": "What does ajal mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q21/p1", "position": "It is the duration or appointed limit of a thing.", "reasons": "Jishumi contrasts ājil with the immediate or present and gives the lexical time sense."}]}
{"id": "6:128/q22", "question": "Does reaching the term imply one fixed lifespan?", "turns_on": "Whether the confession disproves separate terms for natural death, killing, or resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q22/p1", "position": "Yes: everyone, including one murdered, dies at the appointed term.", "reasons": "Al-Jubba'i argues that otherwise a murdered person could not say 'we reached our term'; Razi reports this inference, and Abu Hayyan uses the admission against a doctrine of two terms."}, {"id": "6:128/q22/p2", "position": "No: the verse does not rule out different terms.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Isa and other Baghdadi theologians allow death and resurrection terms or actual death versus a possible full lifespan.
